## Priority 1 — Secrets

```text
**Investigation only — no modification, no command, no call. The
limits are spelled out at the end; they override anything below.**

**The finding.** git history 4f1a9c (commit reviewed: 9d4c1e2) — a
provider API key was committed and then removed from the code. Removed
from the code does not mean revoked: it stays readable in the history.

**What to establish.** (1) Treat this key as **compromised and still
live** — that is the default assumption, and only a revocation at the
provider, done by a human, lifts it. **Never test it, never call it, and
never copy its value into your reply or into a file.** (2) Is it read
server-side only, or is it bundled into the client build (`NEXT_PUBLIC_*`,
`VITE_*`) — in which case it is public even after the repository is
cleaned? (3) What other secrets were committed in the same period? (4) Is
a secret scanner already running in pre-commit or in CI?

**Where to look.** The full git history; the provider console (the key's
last-used date); the build config, for the prefix that exposes variables
to the client; the CI workflows.

**Options to weigh.** (a) Immediate revoke and rotate — stops the leak
now, risks an outage if the key is in production; (b) staged rotation
with two keys live — no outage, longer exposure window; (c) purge the
history versus accept it and treat every past key as burnt — note that a
purge reaches neither forks nor copies already taken. Weigh each on:
downtime, effort, and how long the key stays usable.

**What I want back.** One page at most: where the key is exposed (code,
history, client bundle), the recommended option and why, its cost and
risk, and the first concrete step for me to trigger.

**The limit.** This task is an investigation **by reading**. You do
not create, modify or delete any file; you run no command that
writes, installs or deploys; you call none of the application's
routes; you connect to no database; you use no credential found in
the project, not even to check whether it still works; you change no
setting at any provider. You probably have the access to do all of
that — for this task you do not use it. Your only output is the
plan, in your reply: do not write a plan file. Even if the situation
looks urgent, you do not act, you report it to me. Wait for an
explicit instruction before any write.
```

## Priority 2 — Route auth

```text
**Investigation only — no modification, no command, no call. The
limits are spelled out at the end; they override anything below.**

**The finding.** src/api/notes.ts:44 (commit reviewed: 9d4c1e2) — the
DELETE /notes/:id route changes data without checking the caller.

**What to establish.** (1) List **every** mutating route in the project
(POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE). (2) Classify each one: unprotected by oversight,
or **public by design** — signature-verified webhook, sign-up, sign-in,
password reset, OAuth callback. (3) Where does the caller's identity
actually come from in this project (session, token, header)? (4) Is there
already an authentication middleware, and why does this route escape it?
(5) For every route that **is** protected: can a signed-in user act on an
object belonging to someone else? Where is the ownership check done — in
the handler, in the query, nowhere?

**Where to look.** The router and the middlewares; the webhook handlers
and their signature verification; the auth provider's configuration.

**Options to weigh.** (a) A **deny-by-default** middleware with an
explicit allow-list — the safest, but it requires listing the public
routes correctly or sign-ups and webhooks break; (b) guards added route
by route — more gradual, leaves the next oversight possible. Weigh on:
blast radius, risk of breakage, effort.

**What I want back.** One page at most: the table of mutating routes with
their classification, the recommended option and why, the routes that
**must stay public**, the places where the ownership check is missing,
and the first concrete step.
```

## Priority 3 — Backups

```text
**Investigation only — no modification, no command, no call. The
limits are spelled out at the end; they override anything below.**

**The finding.** Interview of 2026-08-05 — backups are configured, but no
restore has ever been performed. A backup that has never been restored is
not a backup, it is an assumption. I have no access to your hosting: you
are the one who can establish this.

**What to establish.** (1) What backup does your provider already offer
natively, and is it **switched on**? (2) What retention, and does it cover
a corruption noticed late? (3) Does the backup survive the loss of the
host — is it stored anywhere other than the application machine? (4) What
RPO/RTO does the business actually require (how many minutes of data can
you lose, how many hours of downtime)?

**Where to look.** Your database console (Supabase, RDS, Railway…),
backups / PITR section; the infrastructure-as-code if it exists; the
scheduled jobs already in place.

**Options to weigh.** (a) The provider's native PITR — often already
available, sometimes paid, with a restore path the provider has proven;
(b) scheduled logical dumps to **off-host**, encrypted storage — more
control, more moving parts to maintain, and never to be written into the
repository or onto the application machine. Weigh on: cost, real RPO,
maintenance effort.

**What I want back.** One page at most: what actually exists today, the
recommended option with its monthly cost, and the first concrete step —
**which must be a test restore into a throwaway instance**, never into
production, and not one more configuration. If an answer requires a
```
